title: Delhi HC Keeps Project Cost Cap Intact, Strips NHAI Concessionaire of ₹911 Crore Termination Payment
meta_description: Delhi High Court partly sets aside an arbitral award against NHAI, holding the concession agreement's cost cap governs the termination payment claim.
bench: Single Judge (OMP(COMM) proceedings; name not confirmed in available reports)
case_name: National Highways Authority of India v. Kurukshetra Expressway Private Limited
citation: Delhi High Court, OMP(COMM), order dated 28 July 2026, reaffirmed by order dated 28 September 2026
body: Kurukshetra Expressway Private Limited, the concessionaire for the Rohtak-Bawal stretch of NH-71, had its concession terminated after the project ran into back to back disruptions, first the COVID-19 lockdowns and then a farmers' agitation that blocked work on the ground for extended periods. When a concession ends in circumstances the contract treats as force majeure or an NHAI default, the concession agreement provides a formula for working out what NHAI owes the concessionaire as a termination payment, built around the project cost actually incurred. KEPL took that dispute to arbitration and did well there.

A three member tribunal, by majority, awarded KEPL about Rs 911.13 crore under its termination payment claim, with interest running on top of that sum under a connected claim. NHAI's position throughout was that the tribunal had computed the termination payment on a project cost figure that exceeded what the concession agreement itself permitted, effectively letting KEPL recover more than the contract's own cost ceiling allowed regardless of what was actually spent. NHAI challenged the award under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act in December 2024, asking the Delhi High Court to set aside the termination payment portion.

The single judge agreed with NHAI on that specific point. The judgment upheld a Rs 650 crore cap on project cost built into the concession agreement, and held that the tribunal's termination payment figure could not stand because it had been worked out on a cost base the parties' own contract did not permit. On that footing, the order set aside the termination payment award and the interest claimed on it, while expressly leaving every other claim KEPL had won before the tribunal untouched. NHAI's challenge succeeded narrowly, on the one claim where the court found the tribunal had gone beyond the contractual ceiling, not on the broader question of whether KEPL was entitled to compensation at all.

That distinction matters because a Section 34 court is not supposed to re-weigh the merits of an arbitral award the way an ordinary appellate court would. The judge's reasoning turned on contract interpretation rather than on second guessing the tribunal's assessment of disputed facts, which is the narrow lane patent illegality review is meant to occupy. By confining the interference to the termination payment claim and its interest, while upholding the tribunal's findings on every other head, the order tracks that limited role closely rather than opening up the whole award for fresh scrutiny.

KEPL did not accept the outcome quietly. Kalpataru Projects International, KEPL's parent, told stock exchanges that the company believed it had strong grounds to challenge the finding and intended to take further legal steps. Those steps culminated in a second order from the same court on 28 September 2026, which upheld the July ruling rather than disturbing it. The company again informed the exchanges that it considers the order wrong and is preparing an appeal under Section 37 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, which would take the dispute to a Division Bench.

Highway concession agreements almost always build in a project cost ceiling of this kind precisely because NHAI wants certainty over its maximum exposure on termination, whatever the actual circumstances of the termination turn out to be. This ruling shows that ceiling will be read strictly against a concessionaire even where the termination itself was driven by events, a pandemic and a farmers' protest, that nobody seriously disputes were outside the concessionaire's control. A tribunal's sympathy for a concessionaire who lost years of work to force majeure does not translate into licence to exceed a cost cap the contract fixed in advance.

For concessionaires pursuing termination payment claims on NHAI and other public authority contracts, the practical lesson is to anchor the quantum argument in the concession agreement's own cost ceiling from the outset of arbitration, rather than relying on the tribunal's assessment of actual project cost to carry the day if that assessment runs past the ceiling. For NHAI and comparable authorities, the order offers a template for resisting large termination awards without having to contest liability itself, by isolating the one component of the award that strayed past an express contractual limit and attacking only that.
why_it_matters: Highway concession agreements commonly cap the project cost base used to calculate termination payments, and this ruling confirms that an arbitral tribunal cannot award a termination payment exceeding that contractual cap even where the termination itself resulted from acknowledged force majeure. Concessionaires structuring termination payment claims, and authorities defending them, now have a concrete precedent for isolating and contesting only the cost-cap component of an award rather than litigating liability afresh.
card_summary: Delhi High Court sets aside the Rs 911 crore termination payment awarded to KEPL against NHAI, holding the concession agreement's Rs 650 crore cost cap governs, leaving other findings intact.
card_tip: In a termination payment claim under a concession agreement, check whether the computation respects any express project cost ceiling before quantum is finalised in arbitration.
verification_notes: The identity of the parties (NHAI and Kurukshetra Expressway Private Limited, a Kalpataru Projects International joint venture, on the Rohtak-Bawal NH-71 stretch), the COVID-19 and farmers' agitation background to termination, the majority arbitral award of about Rs 911.13 crore as termination payment plus interest, NHAI's Section 34 challenge filed December 2024, the Delhi High Court's 28 July 2026 order setting aside the termination payment and interest claims while upholding the award on all other claims, the court's reliance on a Rs 650 crore project cost cap in the concession agreement, and the 28 September 2026 order upholding the July ruling are corroborated across Raw Law, PSU Connect, Sahi and Equitybulls/ScanX reports as well as the company's own stock exchange filings. The name of the single judge who passed either order could not be confirmed from the available secondary reports and has accordingly been omitted rather than guessed, as has the exact OMP(COMM) case number.
